🇨🇳 China's AI labs are losing their back door to Nvidia chips. One Shanghai investor calls it their "darkest hour". For two years, China's leading AI developers kept pace with American rivals partly by renting Nvidia chips in data centers abroad. That route is closing, and the industry is starting to say so out loud.

Washington now requires data centers to obtain a US license before renting large amounts of computing power to Chinese clients. Add the measures OpenAI and Anthropic have taken against "distillation," training a model on a stronger model's answers, and the result is a "total lockdown" in the short term, Shanghai venture capitalist Bob Chen told AFP. A post he wrote titled "China's AI Models Face Their Darkest Hour" spread widely among insiders before it was taken down.

The strain is showing up in release schedules. Moonshot AI, maker of the Kimi models, has reportedly canceled a deal of 150 million dollars to use Blackwell chips through Indonesia, and Zhipu AI has pushed its next flagship model from this month to next year or later, according to foreign reports compiled by South Korea's Seoul Economic Daily. Tencent President Martin Lau told investors this month that "every company in China will be affected." The Institute for Progress, a US think tank, estimated in October that 46 percent of the computing used by Chinese AI firms ran on Nvidia chips in overseas data centers or smuggled into China.

Lenders are nervous too. A loan increase of 6.6 billion dollars for a Bain Capital-owned data center operator in Malaysia whose clients include ByteDance has been suspended while some banks run extra checks, the Korean paper reported.

The long-term effect may cut the other way. Alibaba says its T-Head chip unit will be able to train models on in-house chips by early next year, and DeepSeek is reportedly training its next flagship on Huawei hardware. Zhang Yi of the research firm iiMedia told AFP that once China's chips and software mature together, the shift away from Nvidia will become irreversible.

Sources: AFP, Seoul Economic Daily

AI news today, 28 November 2026.

Nvidia has told manufacturing partners such as Dell and Supermicro to stop shipping servers with its chips to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, according to the Financial Times. Chinese AI developers have been renting advanced Nvidia compute through cloud providers in the region. A new US Commerce rule gives those providers 90 days to get a licence by proving their end users aren't restricted. Nvidia booked $104bn of revenue through its Singapore subsidiary in 2025. It is unclear whether the halt is temporary.

OpenAI posted a preprint claiming to disprove the polynomial Hirsch conjecture, which bounds how many steps the simplex method's edge walk can need. OpenAI says the main statements are formalised in Lean. Independent expert review is still pending.

Meta declined the UK Financial Conduct Authority's offer to test its Muse agent in a supervised sandbox before the UK launch, WIRED reports. Meta says it engaged constructively with regulators.

OpenAI fixed a billing error that undercounted GPT-6.2 usage. The same work now reaches limits 40% faster on Astra and 25% faster on Sol, with one banked reset for paid users.

Canada expanded its AI Compute Access Fund by C$700 million to C$1 billion, covering up to 80% of costs on Canadian-owned clouds and none for services hosted abroad.

As someone who runs AI platforms for students across India, I read this as one story. Compute is turning into geography. Where your workloads run, and under whose rules, is becoming a product decision, not just an infra one.

Plan for the rules, not just the benchmarks. Judgment > tools.

Sources: Financial Times (25 Nov 2026), Reuters (26 Nov 2026); OpenAI math repository (24 Nov 2026); WIRED (26 Nov 2026); BleepingComputer (26 Nov 2026); Government of Canada (26 Nov 2026).

🤖 TechiesHub AI Daily #10 | 28 Nov 2026

Google makes MCP the front door to Workspace, OpenAI corrects a GPT-6.2 billing bug, and Microsoft shows how attackers are running AI agent frameworks. What developers should know:

1. Google made Workspace MCP servers and the official Workspace CLI generally available, covering Gmail, Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Chat and Tasks. From 1 February 2027, AI agents must reach Workspace through MCP or the CLI rather than calling REST APIs directly. Admins get agent controls, confirmation rules for sensitive actions and agent audit logs.
2. OpenAI fixed a billing bug that over-discounted GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol usage. Users now hit limits 40% faster on Astra and 25% faster on Sol than last week, with no retroactive charges. Go, Plus, Pro and Business subscribers get an extra usage reset, and Business users get free Fast Mode through the end of 2026.
3. Claude Code 2.1.332 adds a PreSkillShellCommand hook event, an OpenTelemetry assistant_response event and skills from MCP servers shown as server:skill, along with many reliability fixes.
4. Microsoft Threat Intelligence detailed how state-backed groups, including Salt Typhoon and Onyx Sleet, use ARTEX, a multi-agent AI penetration testing framework. One campaign logged over 151,000 failed sign-ins, peaking at 2,900 per minute. Microsoft recommends phishing-resistant MFA, rate limiting, secret scanning and decoys.
5. Cloudflare launched Search for Agents in beta. One switch indexes a site and serves Markdown search results to AI agents at /.well-known/search, on all plans.
6. Policy: the Financial Times reports Nvidia told server partners to halt shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia after new US export controls aimed at Chinese firms renting GPUs from overseas cloud providers.

Dev takeaway: if your agents touch Gmail, Drive or Calendar, plan the move from raw REST calls to Workspace MCP or the CLI before 1 February 2027, and harden internet-facing apps with rate limits and phishing-resistant MFA.

Should every SaaS app force AI agents through MCP?

2027–2028: FALLING ALUMINIUM PRICES — A HIDDEN OPPORTUNITY FOR SAUDI ARABIA AND THE UAE?

What if falling aluminium prices become an unexpected competitive advantage for the Middle East while the rest of the world is preparing for another economic slowdown?

There is an interesting contradiction developing in global markets.

Saudi Arabia is investing billions in infrastructure, tourism, residential developments and Vision 2030.

The UAE continues expanding its real estate, financial services, logistics and industrial sectors.

Yet aluminium prices are facing downward pressure as global production capacity expands and the market anticipates a possible supply surplus.

Is this bad news?

Not necessarily.

In fact, it could create an important opportunity for both economies.

But the bigger picture goes far beyond aluminium.

1. CHEAPER ALUMINIUM COULD MEAN MORE COMPETITIVE CONSTRUCTION

Think about what goes into building a modern city:

Residential towers.
Commercial buildings.
Airports and hotels.
Shopping malls.
Industrial facilities.
Data centres and energy infrastructure.

Aluminium is essential for windows, façades, curtain walls, electrical infrastructure and countless construction applications.

If aluminium prices decline while construction activity remains strong, developers could benefit from lower material costs.

Saudi Arabia could improve the economics of major development projects.

The UAE could strengthen its position as a competitive destination for international real estate investment.

But lower material prices do not automatically translate into lower property prices. Financing, land, labour and developer margins also matter.

2. SAUDI ARABIA: TURNING LOWER INPUT COSTS INTO ECONOMIC DIVERSIFICATION

Saudi Arabia has an opportunity to use a period of lower industrial input costs to accelerate infrastructure, manufacturing and downstream industrial development.

The objective should not simply be to build more projects.

It should be to develop a stronger domestic industrial ecosystem.

More local manufacturing, more competitive supply chains, greater industrial productivity and less dependence on imported finished products.

The real opportunity is to capture more value from every dollar invested.

3. UAE: THE ADVANTAGE OF BEING BOTH A PRODUCER AND A CONSUMER

The UAE has a different position.

It is both a major aluminium producer and a major consumer of industrial materials.

Companies such as Emirates Global Aluminium are important to the country’s industrial and export economy.

This creates two opposing effects:

Lower aluminium prices can benefit construction companies and downstream manufacturers.

But they can also reduce revenue and margins for primary aluminium producers.

The opportunity for the UAE is to move further up the value chain:

From producing raw aluminium to manufacturing higher-value products, developing industrial capabilities and expanding international market access.

The real competitive advantage is not simply producing more aluminium. It is creating more economic value from every tonne produced.

4. THE GLOBAL SUPPLY EQUATION: CHINA AND INDONESIA

China’s production capacity constraints and Indonesia’s expanding aluminium industry are changing the global supply landscape.

If new production enters the market faster than consumption grows, aluminium prices could remain under pressure during 2027.

This could benefit major aluminium-consuming economies, but challenge producers competing on margins.

The important question is whether global demand from construction, electrification, electric vehicles, power grids and AI infrastructure can absorb this additional capacity.

5. THE US DOLLAR, EURO AND JAPANESE YEN: THE FINANCIAL SIDE OF THE STORY

Now connect the commodity market with global currencies.

A stronger US Dollar Index (DXY) can create additional pressure on dollar-priced commodities.

A weaker euro changes European purchasing power and the competitiveness of European industry.

Meanwhile, Japanese monetary normalisation could change the attractiveness of domestic bonds versus overseas investments.

Japan’s position in US Treasury markets also deserves attention.

If Japanese investors increasingly find domestic yields attractive, international bond allocation decisions could change.

This may influence US Treasury yields, global financing costs, real estate investment and capital flows.

For Saudi Arabia and the UAE, the cost and availability of international capital are just as important as the price of construction materials.

6. OIL, ENERGY AND GEOPOLITICS: THE FACTORS THAT COULD REVERSE THE TREND

Oil revenues influence government investment capacity.

Energy costs influence aluminium production economics.

And geopolitical disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz can affect shipping, energy exports, industrial production and regional supply chains.

A global market expecting aluminium oversupply could quickly change direction if major supply disruptions occur.

This is why falling aluminium prices should not automatically be interpreted as a long-term bearish signal.

7. MY OUTLOOK FOR 2027–2028

I see three possible outcomes:

SCENARIO A — THE GOLDEN OPPORTUNITY

Aluminium prices decline moderately, construction investment remains strong, and Saudi Arabia and the UAE use lower input costs to accelerate real estate, infrastructure and manufacturing.

This could be the most favourable scenario for regional economic diversification.

SCENARIO B — THE GLOBAL OVERSUPPLY TRAP

New production capacity increases faster than demand.

Aluminium prices fall further, putting pressure on smelter profitability, industrial investment and commodity-producing economies.

Developers may benefit from cheaper inputs, but weaker global demand could undermine the wider economic outlook.

SCENARIO C — THE GEOPOLITICAL REVERSAL

Energy prices rise, shipping routes face disruption and aluminium supply becomes constrained.

Prices recover sharply, increasing costs for construction and manufacturing.

The countries with reliable energy, competitive production and resilient supply chains could gain a significant advantage.

⸻

MY FINAL THOUGHT

I believe the most interesting opportunity for Saudi Arabia and the UAE in 2027–2028 is not simply benefiting from lower aluminium prices.

It is using this potential commodity correction to strengthen their economic foundations.

Cheaper industrial inputs.

More competitive construction.

Stronger local manufacturing.

Higher-value aluminium production.

More resilient supply chains.

Greater economic diversification.

But there is one condition: lower commodity prices must come from improving supply economics, not from a collapse in global demand.

A country that can build more competitively, manufacture more efficiently and attract capital at the right time may gain an advantage over economies that are still paying yesterday’s prices.

The question I would put to investors, developers and policymakers:

Could falling aluminium prices become one of the unexpected economic advantages for Saudi Arabia and the UAE in 2027–2028?

Or are we looking at an early warning of a much bigger global economic slowdown?

Another valuable milestone in my journey as an Electrical Engineer!

I had the opportunity to participate in the Factory Acceptance Test (FAT) of Control Relay Panels (CRP) and Substation Automation System (SAS) for a 150 kV Gas Insulated Substation (GIS) alongside Dani Kusuma Pratama, conducted at Schneider Electric, Karawang, Indonesia, representing PT. Arfy Reka Cerdas as an engineering consultant.

Successfully completed a series of Factory Acceptance Test (FAT) activities for Control Relay Panels (CRP) and Substation Automation Systems (SAS) at Schneider Electric.

The FAT activities covered several panels and systems, including:
1. Transformer Control & Protection Panel
2. Busbar Protection Panel
3. Bus Coupler & Bus Section Panel
4. Underground Cable (UGC) Protection Panel
5. Common IED IO Panel
6. Substation Automation System (SAS) Panel

Scope of Testing & Verification:
✅ Visual Inspection & Mechanical Check
✅ Electrical Check & Wiring Continuity Verification
✅ General Functional Check
✅ Bay Control Unit (BCU) – BI/BO/LED Testing
✅ Automatic Voltage Regulator (AVR) Testing
✅ Main Protection Unit (MPU) Testing
✅ Backup Protection Unit (BPU) Testing
✅ Busbar Differential Protection Testing
✅ Circuit Breaker Failure (CBF) Logic Verification

✅ Power Meter Verification
✅ Intertrip & Tripping Scheme Verification
✅ HMI Signal, Indication & Alarm Verification
✅ Substation Automation System (SAS) Functional Testing

This experience further strengthened my technical understanding of power system protection, control schemes, interlocking logic, and the integration of protection and automation systems within high-voltage substations.

FAT is not merely a testing activity, but a critical engineering milestone in ensuring system reliability, operational safety, and readiness prior to site installation and commissioning.

Grateful for the collaboration, technical discussions, and knowledge sharing with all engineers and stakeholders involved throughout the FAT process.
Every test is a step closer to a safer, more reliable, and intelligent power system. ⚡

10 years. 5 service hubs. Drilling depths from 29 meters to 152 meters.

When we founded Xuzhou Jiuman Machinery Technology Co., Ltd. in 2016, we started with a straightforward goal: build rotary Kelly bars tough enough for China's hardest high-speed rail, bridge, and tunnel foundations—and back them with real field service, not just a shipping invoice.

A decade later, in 2026, that same engineering discipline is supporting deep foundation projects far beyond Xuzhou:

• Interlocking (JS377–JS630) and Friction (MZ406–MZ630) Kelly bars engineered for depths up to 152 meters
• Export deliveries working across Indonesia, Malaysia (including East Coast Railway infrastructure), Vietnam, India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, UAE, Turkmenistan, and Canada
• New, inspected used, and fully remanufactured rotary drilling rigs (XR178E, XR220D, XR280E, XR360E, XR400E) tested before dispatch
• ISO 9001 quality management and SGS-audited manufacturing processes from raw alloy tubing to four-layer sea-freight protection

Every contractor we partner with—from a single-rig specialist in Southeast Asia to multi-rig infrastructure fleets in the Middle East and North America—asks for the same three things: honest specs, reliable lead times, and steel that holds up when the geology turns ugly.

Thank you to every client, engineer, and partner who has trusted Jiuman Machinery over the last 10 years. We're just getting started.

If you work in deep foundations, geotechnical contracting, or heavy equipment trading, let's connect and follow along as we share more project cases, technical guides, and behind-the-scenes builds from our Xuzhou factory: https://jmachglobal.com/

Innovation is our way of creating added value, and the Innovation Awards give us renewed energy to keep bringing our innovations to life. We are proud to be named one of the Top 4 nominees out of 100 innovations across all categories at the Bio Farma Innovation Challenge 2026, and to receive the Good Improvement 1 Award, an achievement that belongs to the entire team!

NVT AI is an AI-based solution designed to accelerate and optimize Neurovirulence Testing (NVT). Evaluation that originally relied on manual microscopy, involving tens of thousands of fragile physical glass slides, is moving to AI-assisted digital evaluation.

We have completed the digitization of physical glass slides using a high-throughput scanner, producing high-resolution Whole Slide Images. This has established a strong data foundation, with more than 10,000 slides now digitally archived.

Bio Farma - Indonesia has also initiated the development of a new validation and regulatory framework for AI implementation. We expect this framework to be adoptable for other AI solutions requiring regulatory approval, another direct contribution to the wider community.

Our special appreciation goes to our outstanding PathologistsSiti Vanessa Fransiska Hedira Aisyah Hiksamdaning Mahyumi Impian Nathasya, AI & Infra Engineer Ahmad Alfi Adz-Dzikri, Digital & Information Technology Division, Idzni Harashta Haifa and International Relations Division, all our partners, and all end users across the QC team. Great work, everyone!

posts.text:
Earlier this month we hosted the first AWS Indonesia Observability Day in Jakarta! 🇮🇩

CloudOps engineers, SREs, architects and IT leaders from across Indonesia spent the day with us on where operations is heading: from monitoring to AI-led, agentic operations.

✨ Spotlight: Amazon CloudWatch Omni Omni is the next generation of Amazon CloudWatch: an AI-powered observability experience built on open standards, with native OpenTelemetry. It was great to show it live and see how quickly the conversation turned to what teams could do with it in their own environments.

We also covered: 🔹 What's new in AWS Observability 🔹 Application Performance Monitoring (APM) 🔹 Unified Data Store 🔹 GenAI Observability 🔹 AWS DevOps Agent 🔹 A hands-on workshop and quiz to finish the day

What stood out to me: most teams already collect plenty of telemetry. The real challenge is finding the root cause fast enough. That's exactly where Omni and AI-assisted investigation come in.

Thank you to everyone who joined us, and to an amazing team: Attha Surya Dharma Elkana Pariwono Kovan Chandra Triadimas Satria Dhika Isfahan andEko Wajar Hidayat. 🙏

None of this would have happened without our sponsors:Baino Paul from the APJ GTM Specialist team, who brought Observability Day to Indonesia, andWelianthy Sukirman from AWS Enterprise Support Indonesia. 

Looking forward to the next one!

#AWS #Observability #CloudOps #AIOps #AmazonCloudWatch #CloudWatchOmni #OpenTelemetry #AWSEnterpriseSupport #AWSAdaUntukIndonesia

posts.text:
Jakarta, Cairo, Lahore: same dollar salary dream, same next problem.

Kelvin Desman, a software engineer, wrote a guide on Medium for Indonesian developers chasing remote jobs paid in US dollars. His argument: skills are rarely the obstacle. Finding employers that hire from Indonesia and pay in dollars is. And dollar pay "holds its value even when the rupiah weakens."

I agree, and I'd add what comes after the offer letter. Four things I'd tell any developer in an emerging market:

1. Check they can pay your country. Not every payroll or contractor platform supports every country. Ask early.

2. Price the net, not the gross. Platform fees, transfer fees and the exchange spread come off the top.

3. Decide when you convert. Rent is local. Savings don't have to be. Convert what you spend.

4. Keep the paper trail. Contracts and invoices matter when your bank asks where the dollars came from.

The offer is step one. Getting paid is step two, in Jakarta, Cairo or Lahore.

Which one caught you out first: the fees, the timing or the paperwork?

Inspired by Kelvin Desman's piece on Medium, 6 Jul 2026

On 27 October 2007, around 500 bloggers from across Indonesia met at Blitz Megaplex, Grand Indonesia, Jakarta, for Pesta Blogger 2007, the country's first national blogger gathering. The theme was "Suara Baru Indonesia" (A New Voice of Indonesia). Organizing chair Enda Nasution proposed making the day National Bloggers' Day, and Communications Minister Muhammad Nuh declared it on stage.

Why it still matters to me: a lot of what we now call content, online communities and personal branding grew out of those personal blogs. Communities from Makassar, Semarang, Bandung, Padang and other cities that knew each other only through comment sections finally met in person. Writing consistently and honestly built trust long before social media algorithms existed.

My lesson: having your own place on the web to write and share is still worth it, especially for developers and business owners. Platforms change, but the writing and relationships you build stay yours. Does anyone here still blog regularly?

Source: https://lnkd.in/ggPF7rtC
